questions.question: A large square is cut into 1000 equal small parts, and the whole square is 1. Exactly 7 of the small parts are shaded. Which decimal names the shaded amount?
questions.explain: One whole is 1000 thousandths, so 7 of those parts is seven thousandths, written 0.007 with the 7 in the third place after the point. The common trap is writing 0.7 or 0.07, which say seven tenths or seven hundredths — much bigger pieces.

questions.question: A paper strip stands for 1 whole and is divided into 1000 equal parts. Rowan colours 25 of those parts. Which decimal shows how much of the strip is coloured?
questions.explain: 25 parts out of 1000 is twenty-five thousandths, so the last digit must land in the thousandths place: 0.025. Writing 0.25 says twenty-five hundredths, which would be 250 of the 1000 parts.

questions.question: A garden bed is one whole unit and is split into 1000 equal squares. Exactly 406 of the squares have seeds in them. Which decimal tells what part of the bed has seeds?
questions.explain: 406 out of 1000 is four hundred six thousandths: 4 tenths, 0 hundredths, 6 thousandths, written 0.406. The trap is dropping the zero to get 0.46, because that moves the 6 into the hundredths place and changes the number.

questions.question: A cardboard sheet is 1 whole and is divided into 1000 equal pieces. Nia colours 60 of the pieces. Which choice writes the coloured amount as a decimal AND names the place of the digit 6 correctly?
options: 0.6, and the 6 is in the tenths place
0.006, and the 6 is in the thousandths place
0.060, and the 6 is in the thousandths place
0.060, and the 6 is in the hundredths place
questions.explain: 60 thousandths is the same as 6 hundredths, so it is 0.060 and the 6 sits in the second place after the point, the hundredths place. A common trap is calling every digit in a thousandths number a 'thousandth' — the place depends on the position, not on how the number was counted.

questions.question: Look at the number 4.517. What is the value of the digit 1?
options: one hundredth (0.01)
one tenth (0.1)
one thousandth (0.001)
one whole (1)
questions.explain: Count the places after the decimal point: 5 is tenths, 1 is hundredths, 7 is thousandths, so the 1 is worth 0.01. Many students grab the first place they think of and call it a tenth — always count the places in order.

questions.question: Ms. Chan asks the class to write 'three and forty-eight thousandths' as a decimal. Which one is correct?
questions.explain: 'Thousandths' means the last digit must sit in the third place after the point, so 48 thousandths needs a zero holding the tenths place: 3.048. Writing 3.48 puts the 4 in the tenths place, which reads as forty-eight hundredths instead.

questions.question: A water bottle in the school gym holds 0.375 L. How is the number 0.375 read out loud?
options: three hundred seventy-five hundredths
three hundred seventy-five tenths
three hundred seventy-five thousandths
thirty-seven and five tenths
questions.explain: The last digit, 5, is in the third place after the point, so the whole decimal is read by that last place: three hundred seventy-five thousandths. Saying 'hundredths' is the usual slip — that name belongs to a number with only two digits after the point.

questions.question: In science class Mai weighs a rock and records 2.906 kg. Which digit is in the hundredths place?
questions.explain: After the decimal point the places go tenths, hundredths, thousandths, so 9 is tenths, 0 is hundredths and 6 is thousandths — the hundredths digit is 0. The trap is skipping the zero and naming 9 or 6, because a zero still holds a real place.

questions.question: At a Grade 5 track meet, Priya's long jump is recorded as 2.075 m. She says, 'The 7 stands for seven hundredths of a metre and the 5 stands for five thousandths of a metre.' Which statement about Priya is correct?
options: Yes — the 7 stands for 0.07 m and the 5 stands for 0.005 m.
No — both digits are part of a thousandths number, so the 7 is 0.007 m and the 5 is 0.005 m.
No — the 7 stands for 0.007 m and the 5 stands for 0.05 m.
No — the 7 stands for 0.7 m, because it is the first digit written after the decimal point.
questions.explain: Read the places in order: 0 is tenths, 7 is hundredths (0.07 m) and 5 is thousandths (0.005 m), so Priya is right. The usual error is assuming the first digit you notice after the point is tenths, or that every digit in a thousandths number is worth a thousandth.

questions.question: A recipe card at home says to add 0.125 kg of butter. Nolan has to read the amount out loud and also name the place of the digit 2. Which choice gets both parts right?
options: one hundred twenty-five hundredths, and the 2 is in the tenths place
one hundred twenty-five thousandths, and the 2 is in the hundredths place
one hundred twenty-five thousandths, and the 2 is in the tenths place
twelve and five thousandths, and the 2 is in the ones place
questions.explain: The last digit is three places after the point, so the number reads as one hundred twenty-five thousandths, and counting places gives 1 tenths, 2 hundredths, 5 thousandths. Students often name the number correctly but then call the 2 a tenth — the name of the whole decimal and the place of one digit are two different things.

questions.question: Leo's group measures a paper clip and writes 1.004 g. Leo says, 'That is really the same as 1.4 g, because extra zeros after the point do not change anything.' What should his partner tell him?
options: Leo is right — zeros written after a decimal point never change the value, so 1.004 and 1.4 are the same mass.
Leo is wrong — 1.004 g is one and four hundredths, so the right short form is 1.04 g, not 1.4 g.
Leo is wrong — 1.004 g is one and four thousandths, but 1.4 g is one and four tenths, a much heavier clip.
Leo is right, as long as he reads 1.004 as 'one and four tenths', because the 4 is the only digit that counts.
questions.explain: Zeros between the decimal point and a digit are place holders: they push the 4 into the thousandths place, so 1.004 and 1.4 are very different amounts. Only zeros on the very end, like 1.400, leave a value unchanged.

questions.question: At a measuring station, a student records the length of a pencil as a decimal with 3 in the ones place, 0 in the tenths place, 8 in the hundredths place and 2 in the thousandths place. Which measurement did the student record?
questions.explain: Build the number place by place: 3 ones, then 0 tenths, 8 hundredths and 2 thousandths gives 3.082 cm. The trap is leaving out the zero and writing 3.82, which slides the 8 up into the tenths place and makes the pencil much longer.
